analysis.one_liner: Requires annual public reporting on how many offshore oil wells and pipelines are actually being plugged and cleaned up.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote, so no annual decommissioning report was ever required.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Interior Department to publish a yearly report on decommissioning offshore oil and gas infrastructure: how many wells, platforms, and pipelines companies were required to plug or remove, how many were actually decommissioned on time, how many were left in place, and what enforcement penalties were issued. The point is to expose how much of the cleanup bill for offshore drilling the industry is shifting to taxpayers and the environment. It never received a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, coastal communities, and environmental advocates would benefit from public, annual disclosure of how many offshore wells, platforms, and pipelines the oil and gas industry is legally required to decommission but has not — infrastructure that leaks or fails and can leave cleanup costs with the public. The data would also help Congress and regulators target enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: Each annual report would have to disclose how many wells, platforms, and pipelines missed their legal decommissioning deadlines, how many were left in place, and what enforcement penalties the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement actually issued.

The reports would be posted publicly on the Interior Department's website, not just delivered to Congress, so taxpayers could see for themselves which companies are leaving infrastructure behind for the public to eventually pay for.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies and their regulators would bear the cost: the industry would face public documentation of missed decommissioning deadlines and weak enforcement, and the Interior Department would take on the administrative work of compiling the annual report.

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires annual reporting; it does not itself force companies to plug wells, shorten deadlines, or raise the financial assurance bonds they must post, so a stubborn backlog could continue even with full publicity.
The first report would not be due until two years after enactment, and the added federal reporting and website work carries a modest administrative cost with no dedicated funding specified.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill itself is modest but useful: it would make hidden decommissioning backlogs and enforcement records public at minimal cost, making it harder for regulators to quietly go easy on oil companies that leave wells unplugged. Its main weakness is that reporting alone does not compel anyone to plug wells or pay for it — it is transparency, not enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Peter Welch introduced the Plug Offshore Wells Act on December 12, 2024, in the final weeks of the 118th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because the bill was never reported out of committee or voted on, no annual decommissioning report requirement was created.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators benefit, since no public record of missed decommissioning deadlines or weak enforcement will be compiled and posted.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring annual public reporting on offshore decommissioning.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: No organized support appeared for the bill; its reporting requirements would have publicly documented industry decommissioning delays and enforcement lapses.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, never scheduling a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsor and three cosponsors were all Democrats, and it died in a committee where no hearing was held.

industries.note: The bill would put public numbers on how often these companies miss decommissioning deadlines and face (or avoid) enforcement, creating reputational and political pressure on the industry. It would not directly force spending, so the cost to the industry is transparency rather than money.

industries.industry: Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement / Interior Department
industries.note: The agency would gain a new annual reporting duty but also face public scrutiny of its enforcement record, which regulators may prefer to keep out of view.
